item.title: 🪞 Why does the brain keep selling you a new "me"?
item.description:
Your “me” is a live build

Heather Berlin, Ethan Kross, and Nicole Vignola (Big Think) argue that a stable “me” is a live mix. Perception mixes internal expectations (what past experience taught you to expect) with external sensory input (what your senses pick up now). Because that mix runs in real time, thoughts, attention, and the story you tell about yourself can change what you feel as “me” tomorrow.

You pull the evidence your mood already wants

Prior experience wires the mind. The brain strengthens the connections that matter and lets others wither (neural pruning). Mood then decides what you notice, and later recall, even when the kitchen has not changed. In a negative headspace you pull more negative evidence; in a positive headspace you pull more positive evidence.

item.title: 🧠🧱 Our stubborn refusal
item.description:
Remember the degree you poured four years and six figures into? Someone shows you data proving that people without the credential are outperforming you, and the degree itself means nothing in your field. You do not say “thank you for the clarity.” You get defensive. You explain why the data misses the deep, unquantifiable value of a proper education.

If you accept their facts, you are not an educated professional anymore. You are just someone who bought a very expensive piece of paper.

item.title: 🧬🧠 Memes jump mind to mind, then make you defend them like identity
item.description:
Coinage

The same coinage: evolutionary biologist Richard Dawkins in The Selfish Gene (1976) built meme from Greek mimema (“that which is imitated”) and shortened it to rhyme with gene, stressing memes as cultural analogues of genes.

What they become

Religions, ideologies, social hierarchies, and shared fictions like money or nation‑states work this way. Once they take root, they guide behavior, attract followers, punish dissent, and defend against criticism.

Old hardware

At a basic level, memes connect to ancient brain circuits like the amygdala and basal ganglia. They trigger fear, belonging, reward, novelty, or identity so defending or sharing them feels meaningful or urgent.
